4.text: The manes of the deer are cut off, together with a narrow strip of skin.

5.text: These are divided into small tufts of hair. Each of the guests pins two pieces

6.text: on his back, one at each shoulder, and wears them until they drop off, as it

7.text: were. A strip of the mane is also often tied to the string of family charms.

8.text: The sacrifice to the fire is performed several times, and the ceremonial

9.text: ends with the “feeding” of the fire of the lamp in the sleeping-room. This

10.text: last ceremony occurs but seldom in the ceremonials of the Reindeer people.

11.text: After the ceremonial, the antlers are taken to the burial-places of the nearest

12.text: relatives, as I shall describe later.

13.text: A wild reindeer-buck killed in the herd at any other season sometimes

14.text: receives a slaughtering-sacrifice: at least, a sacred fire will be lighted near

15.text: the carcass, and a small sacrifice thrown in.

16.text: The black bear, the elk, the wolverene, and the wolf are thought worthy

17.text: of a brief ceremonial of the same kind. All the essential details are repeated,

18.text: including the slaughtering-sacrifice, the sacrifice to the fire, the cooking of

19.text: ceremonial dishes, and bringing the head into the tent, where the people

20.text: greet it with songs and drum-beating. In most cases a special thanksgiving

22.text: I was told that with wolves, and sometimes with black bears, the master

23.text: of the house, when performing the ceremonial, takes the fresh skin and puts

24.text: it on in such a way, that his head is covered with the skin of the animal’s

26.text: carried into the tent. The master of the house, dressed in the wolf-skin, per-

29.text: pretending that the spirit of the wolf has entered his body. In the wolf

32.text: These ceremonials, however, are performed chiefly in the fall. If the

33.text: animals named are killed in the spring, they are brought home with simply

34.text: the ceremony of “giving a drink,”² in which a drink is offered to the carcass.

35.text: Some of the Reindeer Chukchee treat in a similar manner stray seals which

36.text: happen to be taken by them at this season. Others store the heads of seals,

37.text: and afterwards perform the thanksgiving ceremonial over them. The Maritime

38.text: Chukchee store the heads of thong-seals and walrus for summer ceremonials
